Its stated reason is sustainability: recovering the current collectors (Cu and Al) matters because copper smelting is a major source of emissions in the battery life cycle, so it argues that dissolving Al in alkaline solution is "suggesting that dissolving Al" and then "in an alkaline solution is not a sustainable separation method". The review's concern with the alkaline route is that it is not sustainable. Its other comments on alkaline leaching are that it has disadvantages similar to acid leaching, in which waste processing is cost-prohibitive.

rendered: The review does not recommend this. It presents dissolving aluminium foil in an alkaline solution as a poor option. Its stated reason is sustainability: recovering the current collectors (Cu and Al) matters because copper smelting is a major source of emissions in the battery life cycle, so it argues that dissolving Al in alkaline solution is "suggesting that dissolving Al" and then "in an alkaline solution is not a sustainable separation method". The review's concern with the alkaline route is that it is not sustainable. Its other comments on alkaline leaching are that it has disadvantages similar to acid leaching, in which waste processing is cost-prohibitive.[1][2][3][4] For separating cathode coatings from aluminium foil, the review instead points to methods such as detaching the coatings in ethylene glycol, which can delaminate cathode films from Al foil in seconds without corroding the foil. It notes that the PVDF binder was not removed in those studies, which is still a problem for direct recycling.[5][6]
